docs.summary: The overview and hub of a commentary series on the follow-up normative scenario from the authors of AI 2027 (AI Futures Project) — a recommendation rather than a prediction, covering the core idea of delaying superintelligence to 2040 through a US-China agreement, the one-line gist, an interactive timeline and a comparison with AI 2027, and pointing to the three installments on the scenario, the policy and the reactions

relations.evidenceRef: Overview and hub — it sets up the four-part structure and the background (a recommendation, not a forecast), so it precedes the year-by-year scenario detail

docs.name: news-20260709-ai-2040-scenario
docs.title: AI 2040: Plan A — the year-by-year scenario (2027 → 2040)
docs.summary: The world Plan A paints year by year — 2027 two workforces (humans + AI agents), 2028 the election and data center costs, 2029 the US-China agreement, 2030 averting full automation, 2030-35 expansion to expert level, 2035 a pause to keep control, 2040 the release and superintelligence, stated explicitly as a recommendation rather than a prediction

relations.evidenceRef: Assumes the year-by-year world the scenario draws, then reads the policy and verification that hold it up (body: 'Next — policy and verification')

docs.title: AI 2040: Plan A — Policy and Verification
docs.summary: The mechanisms that hold the deal together — total research transparency, the verification protocol (network taps and partial recomputation), SL5 security, relocated data centers (US to Mongolia, China to Canada), mutually assured compute destruction, the model spec and third-party oversight; the original's interactive Supplements explorer is carried here only as a static summary

relations.evidenceRef: After understanding the policy and verification machinery, read the support and criticism it drew (body: 'Next — Reactions and critiques')

docs.summary: A board of support and criticism after the release. Richard Ngo's three objections (the ambiguity of an optimistic forecast, the 2040 handover of power, the politics of optimism, published alongside at the authors' request), Dave Friedman (technical legibility is not political feasibility), Rohit Krishnan (underspecified terms), plus coverage from Scott Alexander, WaPo and Axios
